etymology: From dis- (privative) and quiet, Latin quies, rest. Webster 1828: made uneasy or restless; disturbed; harassed. The word describes not agony but the loss of rest — a soul that cannot settle.
biblical_def: Disquieted is the psalmist’s word for a soul that will not settle, and Scripture puts it three times in the mouth of a believer questioning himself. Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance (Psalm 42:5), repeated at Psalm 42:11 and again at Psalm 43:5 as the refrain of two psalms. The structure is worth noting carefully: the man does not deny that he is disquieted, and he does not wait for the feeling to lift. He interrogates his own soul, refuses its verdict, and preaches to it — hope thou in God — on the ground of a future certainty, I shall yet praise him. That is the biblical handling of a downcast spirit, and it is neither denial nor surrender. The word also has an accusing use. Of the man who spends his life accumulating, the psalm says: Surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain: he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them (Psalm 39:6). Here the disquiet is self-inflicted and pointless — a restless getting for an heir the getter cannot name.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DISQUIETED as made uneasy or restless; disturbed; harassed; deprived of peace or tranquillity of mind.
webster_full: DISQUIETED, pp. — Made uneasy or restless; disturbed; deprived of quiet or tranquillity.
Harassed; vexed; agitated by care, fear, or trouble.
Applied to the mind or soul, denoting the loss of settled rest rather than acute pain.
Also applied to nations and to households in a state of unrest.
From dis-, apart or away, and Latin quies, rest — the root also of quiet, quiescent, and acquiesce.
scriptures: Psalm 42:5
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.
Psalm 42:11
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.
Psalm 43:5
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.
Psalm 39:6
Surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain: he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them.
corruption_summary: The therapeutic account of a downcast spirit asks the sufferer to sit with the feeling and validate it, where the psalmist questions his own soul, contradicts it, and preaches a future certainty to it.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 42 is the model, and its method is unfashionable in two directions at once. It does not suppress: the psalmist admits that his tears have been his meat day and night, that deep calls to deep, that all God’s waves have gone over him. But it does not indulge either. He turns and addresses himself in the second person — Why art thou cast down, O my soul? — and refuses to accept the soul’s account of the situation as final. Martyn Lloyd-Jones built his Spiritual Depression on exactly this observation: most of our unhappiness comes from listening to ourselves instead of talking to ourselves. The remedy prescribed is not a feeling but a fact, held in the future tense: I shall yet praise him.

The dictionary is not indifferent to real affliction, and this psalm forbids indifference. The man is genuinely in the land of Jordan, remembering better days at the house of God with a multitude, and taunted with Where is thy God? Scripture gives such a man permission to say all of it. What it does not give is permission to conclude from his condition that God has changed, and it supplies the discipline of self-address as the ordinary means of resistance. Psalm 39:6 adds the other warning: much of what people call anxiety is the disquiet of accumulation — restless getting for heirs one cannot name — and that species is cured by repentance rather than comfort.
roots_summary: Hebrew hamah (H1993), to murmur, to be in tumult, to be disquieted; shachach (H7817), to be bowed down; ragaz (H7264), to tremble, to be agitated; Greek tarasso (G5015), to trouble, to stir up.
roots_lines: Hebrew hamah (H1993) — to murmur, roar, be in commotion; why art thou disquieted in me? (Psalm 42:5).
Hebrew shachach (H7817) — to be bowed down, to sink; the companion verb, rendered cast down.
Hebrew ragaz (H7264) — to quiver, to be agitated; surely they are disquieted in vain (Psalm 39:6).
Greek tarasso (G5015) — to agitate, to trouble; Let not your heart be troubled (John 14:1).
Greek merimnao (G3309) — to be anxious, to be divided in mind; Take no thought for your life (Matthew 6:25).
usage: Why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God (Psalm 42:5) — the soul questioned and then preached to.
I shall yet praise him (Psalm 42:11) — a future certainty held against a present feeling.
Surely they are disquieted in vain (Psalm 39:6) — restless getting for an heir the getter cannot name.

etymology: From dis- (privative) and courage, Old French corage, from Latin cor, the heart. Webster 1828: deprived of courage; depressed in spirits; disheartened. Literally, un-hearted — the heart taken out of a man.
biblical_def: Discouraged is literally to have the heart taken out, and Scripture records it of a nation, warns fathers against causing it in children, and denies it of the Messiah. Of the nation: they journeyed from mount Hor by the way of the Red sea, to compass the land of Edom: and the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way (Numbers 21:4). It was not the enemy that unhearted them but the route — a detour around Edom, going backward toward the sea they had already crossed — and the murmuring and the fiery serpents follow immediately. Moses had earlier put the command in the plainest terms at the border: Behold, the LORD thy God hath set the land before thee: go up and possess it… fear not, neither be discouraged (Deuteronomy 1:21). Paul names it as the specific damage a father can do: Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged (Colossians 3:21) — the danger to a child under a harsh father is not rebellion but the loss of heart. And Isaiah says of the Servant that He alone will not suffer it: He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law (Isaiah 42:4).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DISCOURAGED as deprived of courage; disheartened; depressed in spirits; deterred or dissuaded from an undertaking by fear or difficulty.
webster_full: DISCOURAGED, pp. — Deprived of courage; disheartened; depressed in spirits.
Deterred or dissuaded from an attempt by fear, difficulty, or the appearance of danger.
Deprived of confidence in the success of an undertaking; dispirited.
Applied to individuals, to armies, and to whole peoples whose resolution has failed.
From dis- and courage, from Latin cor, the heart — the root also of cordial, concord, and record.
scriptures: Numbers 21:4
And they journeyed from mount Hor by the way of the Red sea, to compass the land of Edom: and the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way.
Deuteronomy 1:21
Behold, the LORD thy God hath set the land before thee: go up and possess it, as the LORD God of thy fathers hath said unto thee; fear not, neither be discouraged.
Colossians 3:21
Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged.
Isaiah 42:4
He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law.
corruption_summary: Colossians 3:21 addresses fathers by name and warns of a specific injury — a child un-hearted by provocation — and both the harsh reading of headship that ignores the warning and the abdicating father who reads it as a reason to command nothing miss what Paul wrote.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is addressed to fathers, not to parents generally, and it sits immediately after Children, obey your parents in all things. Paul gives authority and then bounds it, which is the invariable biblical pattern for every office. The injury he names is not resentment but discouragement: a child who has been provoked long enough does not fight, he gives up, and Ephesians 6:4 gives the positive alternative — bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. A complementarian household that quotes the command to children and passes over the command to fathers has taken half a text. The dictionary holds the creational order of headship without reservation and holds this warning with equal force, because Paul joined them in one paragraph.

The opposite failure is now the more common one. Reading the warning as though any exercise of paternal authority risks damaging a child, many fathers command nothing, correct nothing, and leave their households to be discipled by whatever else is available. That is not the avoidance of provocation; it is the abdication Eli was judged for, whose sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not (1 Samuel 3:13). Numbers 21:4 shows the third and quieter source of discouragement, which no one causes: the way itself. Israel lost heart not at a battle but at a detour, which is worth remembering by anyone whose present trouble is merely that the road has gone on longer than expected.
roots_summary: Hebrew qatsar (H7114), to be short, shortened — the soul of the people was shortened; chathath (H2865), to be broken, dismayed; Greek athumeo (G120), to be disheartened, literally without spirit.
roots_lines: Hebrew qatsar (H7114) — to be short, impatient; Numbers 21:4 says literally that the soul of the people was shortened by the way.
Hebrew chathath (H2865) — to be dismayed, broken, shattered; fear not, neither be discouraged (Deuteronomy 1:21).
Hebrew ratsats (H7533) — to crush, to break; He shall not fail in Isaiah 42:4 is from this root, echoing the bruised reed of verse 3.
Greek athumeo (G120) — to be without heart or spirit, to lose courage; only at Colossians 3:21.
Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to faint, to lose heart; let us not be weary in well doing (Galatians 6:9).
usage: The soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way (Numbers 21:4) — unhearted by a detour, not by an enemy.
Fathers, provoke not your children… lest they be discouraged (Colossians 3:21) — authority given and then bounded.
He shall not fail nor be discouraged (Isaiah 42:4) — said of the Servant alone.

etymology: From Latin perplexus, entangled, intricate, from per (thoroughly) and plectere (to weave, to braid). Webster 1828: made intricate; puzzled; embarrassed with doubt. The root image is a knot — threads woven together past the point of untangling.
biblical_def: Perplexed is the state of a man who cannot see his way through, and Paul’s use of it is one of the most precise sentences in the New Testament about Christian suffering: We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair (2 Corinthians 4:8). He concedes the perplexity outright. The apostle does not claim to understand what God is doing; he claims only that being at a loss is not the same as being without hope, and the Greek makes a deliberate play — at a loss, but not utterly at a loss. The word is used of a king who cannot make sense of a report: Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him: and he was perplexed, because that it was said of some, that John was risen from the dead (Luke 9:7). It is used of a whole city under an incomprehensible decree, in one of Scripture’s most chilling contrasts: the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed (Esther 3:15). And Joel uses it of animals in a famine, which is oddly moving: How do the beasts groan! the herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture (Joel 1:18).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PERPLEXED as made intricate or involved; entangled; puzzled; embarrassed with doubt or difficulty; rendered unable to decide or to see the way forward.
webster_full: PERPLEXED, pp. — Made intricate; entangled; involved so that the parts cannot be readily distinguished.
Puzzled; embarrassed with doubt; unable to determine what to think or to do.
Harassed with anxiety or vexation arising from uncertainty.
Applied to affairs, questions, and paths, as well as to persons.
From Latin per, thoroughly, and plecto, to weave — the root also of complex, plait, and pleat.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 4:8
We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;
Luke 9:7
Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him: and he was perplexed, because that it was said of some, that John was risen from the dead;
Esther 3:15
The posts went out, being hastened by the king's commandment, and the decree was given in Shushan the palace. And the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed.
Joel 1:18
How do the beasts groan! the herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture; yea, the flocks of sheep are made desolate.
corruption_summary: Both the triumphalist teaching that a believer walking rightly always understands what God is doing, and the counsel that unresolved bewilderment is grounds for abandoning faith, are refused by a single clause: perplexed, but not in despair.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s four contrasts in 2 Corinthians 4:8-9 are all built the same way — troubled but not distressed, perplexed but not in despair, persecuted but not forsaken, cast down but not destroyed. In every pair the first term is granted in full. He is genuinely at a loss. Against the prosperity and victorious-life teachings, which treat confusion as a symptom of insufficient faith, Paul places bewilderment among the ordinary conditions of apostolic ministry and never suggests it should be resolved before the work continues. The believer is not promised comprehension. He is promised that the treasure is in earthen vessels that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.

The opposite corruption treats the same experience as a verdict. Where a person has been taught that faith means understanding, a season of genuine perplexity presents itself as evidence that the whole thing was false, and the modern deconstruction narrative usually runs through exactly this point. Paul’s distinction is the answer, and it is a real distinction rather than a word game: to be at a loss for the meaning of a providence is one thing; to conclude there is no meaning is another, and nothing compels the second from the first. Esther 3:15 shows what such a moment looks like from the outside — the decree published, the city bewildered, the king drinking — and the book’s whole point is that God’s hand was in it although His name is never mentioned.
roots_summary: Greek aporeo (G639), to be without a way, to be at a loss; exaporeomai (G1820), to be utterly without a way, to despair; Hebrew bok (H943), to be confused, entangled.
roots_lines: Greek aporeo (G639) — to be without passage, at a loss; from a-, not, and poros, a way through.
Greek exaporeomai (G1820) — to be utterly at a loss, to despair; Paul’s deliberate contrast in 2 Corinthians 4:8.
Hebrew bok (H943) — to be confounded, entangled; They are entangled in the land (Exodus 14:3).
Greek diaporeo (G1280) — to be thoroughly perplexed; Herod in Luke 9:7 and the crowd at Pentecost (Acts 2:12).
Greek thlibo (G2346) — to press, to afflict; the troubled on every side of the same verse.
usage: We are perplexed, but not in despair (2 Corinthians 4:8) — the loss granted in full, the conclusion refused.
The king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed (Esther 3:15) — bewilderment seen from outside.
The herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture (Joel 1:18) — even the beasts under a judgment they cannot read.

etymology: From Saxon dim, dark, obscure. Webster 1828: not seeing clearly; having the visual faculty impaired; obscure; not clearly visible. Scripture uses it chiefly of failing eyes, and uses that failing to mark the passing of an age.
biblical_def: Dim in Scripture is almost always said of eyes, and the Bible uses failing sight to mark the ends of things. Isaac’s dimness is the hinge of Genesis 27: when Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim, so that he could not see, he called Esau his eldest son (Genesis 27:1) — and what follows is a blind father deceived by goatskins, blessing the wrong son, and thereby fulfilling the word God had spoken before the twins were born. Eli’s dimness is likewise more than physical: when Eli was laid down in his place, and his eyes began to wax dim, that he could not see (1 Samuel 3:2), and the previous verse has already said that the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision. The old priest cannot see, the nation has no vision, and God calls a boy. Against these stands the extraordinary note about Moses: Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated (Deuteronomy 34:7). Lamentations gives the corporate version: For this our heart is faint; for these things our eyes are dim (Lamentations 5:17). And Isaiah promises the reversal: the eyes of them that see shall not be dim, and the ears of them that hear shall hearken (Isaiah 32:3).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DIM as not seeing clearly; having the visual organs impaired; dull of apprehension; and, of objects, obscure, not clearly seen, or imperfectly illuminated.
webster_full: DIM, a. — Not seeing clearly; having the visual faculty obscured or impaired.
Dull of apprehension; having obscure conceptions; as, a dim understanding.
Not clearly seen; obscure; imperfectly illuminated; as, a dim light or a dim prospect.
Somewhat dark; tarnished; having the lustre obscured; as, gold become dim.
From Saxon dim, dark — connected with dusk and with the sense of shadow rather than of total darkness.
scriptures: Genesis 27:1
And it came to pass, that when Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim, so that he could not see, he called Esau his eldest son, and said unto him, My son: and he said unto him, Behold, here am I.
1 Samuel 3:2
And it came to pass at that time, when Eli was laid down in his place, and his eyes began to wax dim, that he could not see;
Deuteronomy 34:7
And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated.
Lamentations 5:17
For this our heart is faint; for these things our eyes are dim.
Isaiah 32:3
And the eyes of them that see shall not be dim, and the ears of them that hear shall hearken.
corruption_summary: Genesis 27 is often read as a story in which human deceit thwarts or reroutes God’s plan, when Romans 9 cites the very outcome — the younger served by the elder — as the standing proof of unconditional election.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter is full of sin and Scripture does not excuse any of it: Isaac intends to bless Esau against the word God gave Rebekah, Rebekah schemes, Jacob lies outright to his blind father, and Esau plots murder. Yet the result is exactly what God had announced before either child was born — the elder shall serve the younger (Genesis 25:23) — and Paul builds Romans 9 on that announcement to prove that election is not of works, but of him that calleth. The doctrine of concurrence holds both truths without softening either: God ordains the end and the means, and the men who sin in bringing it about are fully guilty. Joseph states the principle for his brothers: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good (Genesis 50:20). A providence that could be defeated by a dish of venison and a pair of goatskins would not be providence.

The Eli narrative supplies a second lesson the church should not miss. His eyes waxing dim is placed alongside the statement that there was no open vision, and the two failures are told as one. He had heard God’s word against his house and restrained his sons anyway not at all; he could not see; and the LORD called a child who did not yet know Him. Deuteronomy 34:7 stands as the deliberate contrast: Moses at a hundred and twenty with undimmed eye and unabated force, because God kept him for the work. Neither man’s eyesight is presented as a merely medical fact. Scripture reads the failing of the senses in old men who lead as a summons to the next generation, and Isaiah 32:3 promises a day when the seeing eyes will not grow dim at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew kahah (H3543), to grow dim, to be faint; keheh (H3544), dim, faint; chashak (H2821), to be dark; Greek ainigma (G135), an enigma — the darkly of 1 Corinthians 13:12.
roots_lines: Hebrew kahah (H3543) — to grow dim, to be faint; used of Isaac’s eyes, Eli’s eyes, and Moses’ eye which did not.
Hebrew keheh (H3544) — dim, faint, colourless; the smoking flax shall he not quench uses the related idea (Isaiah 42:3).
Hebrew chashak (H2821) — to be or grow dark; our eyes are dim (Lamentations 5:17).
Hebrew shaah (H8159) — to gaze, to look; the eyes of Isaiah 32:3 that shall not be dim.
Greek ainigma (G135) — a riddle; now we see through a glass, darkly (1 Corinthians 13:12).
usage: When Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim (Genesis 27:1) — a blind father, a deceived blessing, and God’s word fulfilled anyway.
Eli… his eyes began to wax dim (1 Samuel 3:2) — failing sight set beside a nation with no open vision.
His eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated (Deuteronomy 34:7) — the deliberate contrast, said of Moses at a hundred and twenty.

etymology: From sigh, Saxon sican, to draw a long breath. Webster 1828: the act of sighing; a deep and audible respiration expressing grief or longing. It is grief too deep or too tired for words, and Scripture treats it as prayer God hears.
biblical_def: Sighing is inarticulate grief, and the remarkable thing in Scripture is that God answers it as though it were speech. For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD; I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him (Psalm 12:5). No petition is recorded, no argument is made; there is only sighing, and God says now will I arise. The psalmist elsewhere describes his own life measured out in it: For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of mine iniquity, and my bones are consumed (Psalm 31:10) — and he traces the cause honestly to his own sin, not to circumstance. God can also silence sighing in judgment, which is a terrible thing to read: Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease (Isaiah 21:2), spoken of Babylon, whose oppression of others is being ended by ending Babylon. And the word receives its final answer in one of the great promises: And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away (Isaiah 35:10).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SIGHING as the act of sighing — a deep, long, and audible respiration or single inspiration, occasioned by grief, oppression of the heart, or earnest longing.
webster_full: SIGHING, n. — The act of sighing; a deep and audible respiration expressing grief, weariness, or longing.
SIGH, v.i. — To inhale a larger quantity of air than usual and emit it audibly, as under the pressure of sorrow.
Figuratively, to lament; to mourn; to express grief without words.
In Scripture, often joined with groaning and with crying, as the sound of an oppressed people.
From Saxon sican, to sigh — probably imitative of the sound of the breath.
scriptures: Psalm 12:5
For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD; I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him.
Psalm 31:10
For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of mine iniquity, and my bones are consumed.
Isaiah 21:2
A grievous vision is declared unto me; the treacherous dealer dealeth treacherously, and the spoiler spoileth. Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease.
Isaiah 35:10
And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
corruption_summary: Psalm 12:5 has God arising for the sighing of the needy, and both the prosperity teaching that a sighing believer lacks faith and the religious sentimentality that treats such promises as merely inward comfort miss what the verse says God will do.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is a divine oath in the middle of a psalm about flattering lips and the vanishing of the godly, and its structure is worth attending to. The cause is the oppression of the poor and the sighing of the needy; the response is now will I arise, saith the LORD; the outcome is I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him. No repentance is required of the needy first, no eloquence, no formula. Against the teaching that a believer’s difficulty is evidence of insufficient faith or a negative confession, this psalm has God moved by a sound made by people with nothing left to say. Romans 8:26 continues the pattern into the New Testament: the Spirit makes intercession with groanings which cannot be uttered.

The second corruption reduces the promise to a feeling. Psalm 12:5 says God will set him in safety, and Isaiah 35:10 says the ransomed will come to Zion with everlasting joy on their heads and that sorrow and sighing shall flee away. These are promises of an actual state of affairs, secured by an actual redemption, and consummated in a real new heaven and new earth where God shall wipe away all tears (Revelation 21:4). Read as inward consolation only, they are thin. Read as what they say, they are the ground on which a believer may sigh without pretence and still hope without embarrassment. Psalm 31:10 shows the honest form of it: the psalmist names his own iniquity as the cause and sighs anyway, to the God he has offended.
roots_summary: Hebrew anachah (H585), a sighing, a groaning; anach (H584), to sigh, to groan; naaqah (H5009), a groaning; Greek stenazo (G4727), to groan, to sigh inwardly.
roots_lines: Hebrew anachah (H585) — a sigh, a groan; sorrow and sighing shall flee away (Isaiah 35:10).
Hebrew anach (H584) — to sigh, to groan; the verb behind the sighing of the oppressed.
Hebrew naaqah (H5009) — a groaning; I have heard the groaning of the children of Israel (Exodus 6:5).
Greek stenazo (G4727) — to groan inwardly; we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened (2 Corinthians 5:4).
Greek stenagmos (G4726) — a groaning; the unutterable groanings of the Spirit in Romans 8:26.
usage: For the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD (Psalm 12:5) — God answering a sound, not an argument.
My years with sighing… because of mine iniquity (Psalm 31:10) — grief honestly traced to its cause.
Sorrow and sighing shall flee away (Isaiah 35:10) — the promised end of the sound.

etymology: From laugh, Saxon hlihhan. Webster 1828: convulsive merriment; an expression of mirth peculiar to man. Scripture treats it as both a gift of God in deliverance and a mask over a sorrowful heart, and Ecclesiastes calls it mad.
biblical_def: Laughter in Scripture is neither condemned nor simply commended; it is weighed, and the weighing is unusually shrewd. At its best it is the involuntary response of a delivered people: When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream. Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the heathen, The LORD hath done great things for them (Psalm 126:1-2). That laughter is a form of praise and the nations recognise it as such. But Proverbs observes what laughter often covers: Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness (Proverbs 14:13). The Preacher, who tested every pleasure deliberately, returns a hard verdict: I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it? (Ecclesiastes 2:2), and states the reason elsewhere — Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better (Ecclesiastes 7:3). James applies this pastorally to a worldly church: Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to heaviness (James 4:9), which is a call to repentance rather than to gloom.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LAUGHTER as convulsive merriment; an expression of mirth peculiar to the human species, consisting in a peculiar noise and motion of the muscles of the face and body; also, an expression of scorn or contempt.
webster_full: LAUGHTER, n. — Convulsive merriment; an expression of mirth peculiar to man, attended by a peculiar noise and motion of the features.
The expression of joy or gladness; as, the mouth filled with laughter.
Sometimes an expression of scorn, derision, or contempt; as, to hold a thing in laughter.
Distinguished by moralists from cheerfulness, which is habitual, laughter being sudden and transient.
From Saxon hlehter, from hlihhan, to laugh — probably imitative in origin.
scriptures: Psalm 126:2
Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the heathen, The LORD hath done great things for them.
Proverbs 14:13
Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness.
Ecclesiastes 2:2
I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?
Ecclesiastes 7:3
Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better.
James 4:9
Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to heaviness.
corruption_summary: A church shaped by entertainment has made continuous levity the mark of an approachable ministry, and James 4:9 addresses precisely such a congregation with a command that no modern service would dare to obey.
corruption_paragraphs: James is writing to people with wars and fightings among them, who ask and receive not because they ask amiss, and whom he calls adulterers for their friendship with the world. His prescription is Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to heaviness — followed immediately by Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up. The mourning is not an end but a road, and it leads to being lifted up. Against this, the ordinary evangelical service is engineered so that no one will ever be uncomfortable, and the pulpit’s first duty is understood to be warmth. The dictionary does not commend sourness; Psalm 126 is in the same canon and the laughter there is a mark of God’s work. It observes only that a ministry incapable of producing James 4:9 has removed a tool the apostles used.

Ecclesiastes 7:3 states the principle that makes sense of the whole: by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better. Sorrow does something for a man that mirth cannot, which is why the Preacher says it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting. This is not a preference for misery but an observation about what teaches. Proverbs 14:13 completes it from the other side, and anyone who has watched a room knows it is true: Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful. Laughter is often the sound a grief makes when it is not permitted to be heard, and a church that leaves no room for the house of mourning gives such people nowhere to go.
roots_summary: Hebrew sechoq (H7814), laughter, derision; tsachaq (H6711), to laugh — the root of the name Isaac; Greek gelos (G1071), laughter; gelao (G1070), to laugh.
roots_lines: Hebrew sechoq (H7814) — laughter, and also derision; our mouth filled with laughter (Psalm 126:2).
Hebrew tsachaq (H6711) — to laugh; Sarah laughed, and the son was named Yitschaq, Isaac, he laughs (Genesis 21:6).
Hebrew holelah (H1947) — madness; I said of laughter, It is mad (Ecclesiastes 2:2).
Greek gelos (G1071) — laughter; only at James 4:9 in the New Testament.
Greek gelao (G1070) — to laugh; Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh (Luke 6:21).
usage: Then was our mouth filled with laughter (Psalm 126:2) — the involuntary praise of a delivered people.
Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful (Proverbs 14:13) — the sound a grief makes when it may not be heard.
Let your laughter be turned to mourning (James 4:9) — a call to repentance, and the road to being lifted up.

etymology: From mad, Saxon gemaad, out of one’s mind. Webster 1828: distraction; a state of disordered reason; extreme folly. Scripture uses it for judicial insanity sent from God, for the moral condition of the natural heart, and for the folly of a hired prophet.
biblical_def: Madness in Scripture is more often a moral than a medical term, and its most sobering use makes it the settled condition of the unregenerate heart. The Preacher states it as a general observation about mankind: the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead (Ecclesiastes 9:3). That is not a description of the deranged few; it is a verdict on the race. Solomon had set himself to study the thing deliberately: And I gave my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly: I perceived that this also is vexation of spirit (Ecclesiastes 1:17). Madness is also listed among the covenant curses, sent judicially: The LORD shall smite thee with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart (Deuteronomy 28:28) — the mind itself given over, which the New Testament echoes in the giving over of Romans 1. And Peter uses the word for the specific folly of a prophet who preached for money: the dumb ass speaking with man’s voice forbad the madness of the prophet (2 Peter 2:16). A man who would not hear God heard a donkey, and Peter calls his course madness rather than mere error.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MADNESS as distraction; a state of disordered reason or intellect, in which the patient raves or is furious; and, in a moral sense, extreme folly, rashness, or wildness of conduct proceeding from a disordered heart.
webster_full: MADNESS, n. — Distraction; a state of disordered reason or intellect, in which the person raves or acts furiously.
Extreme folly; headstrong passion and rashness that act in opposition to reason.
Wildness of conduct proceeding from a disordered will rather than a disordered understanding.
In Scripture, sometimes a judicial infliction, God smiting a people with madness and astonishment of heart.
From Saxon gemaad, mad — connected with the sense of being changed or turned out of one’s course.
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 9:3

This is an evil among all things that are done under the sun, that there is one event unto all: yea, also the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
Ecclesiastes 1:17
And I gave my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly: I perceived that this also is vexation of spirit.
Deuteronomy 28:28
The LORD shall smite thee with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart:
2 Peter 2:16
But was rebuked for his iniquity: the dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet.
corruption_summary: Ecclesiastes 9:3 calls madness the condition of every natural heart, which the modern account of human nature as fundamentally good and only situationally damaged cannot accommodate at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is unqualified: the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live. Not some hearts, not damaged hearts, not hearts that suffered badly — the sons of men. This is the doctrine the Reformed tradition calls total depravity, meaning not that every person is as wicked as he could be but that no faculty is untouched, the mind included. Jeremiah 17:9 says the same of the heart’s deceitfulness. Against it stands the therapeutic anthropology in which people are essentially well and behave badly because of what was done to them, so that the remedy is insight and a supportive environment. If that account were true, the incarnation was an overreaction. Scripture’s diagnosis is madness in the heart, and its remedy is a new heart, which only God gives.

Deuteronomy 28:28 raises a harder point, and the dictionary states it plainly rather than around it: madness appears in Scripture among the judicial curses, and Romans 1 describes God giving men over to a reprobate mind. This must not be turned into a rule for reading any particular sufferer’s case — Job’s friends made exactly that mistake, and the man born blind was blind for neither his sin nor his parents’. The believer who suffers illness of mind is not thereby under judgment, and the church that implies it commits real cruelty. What the text establishes is only that the mind is not a sanctuary from God’s government, and that a nation which will not have His law may find its reasoning taken away.
roots_summary: Hebrew holelah (H1947), madness, folly; shiggaon (H7697), madness, raving; Greek paraphronia (G3913), derangement, madness; mania (G3130), madness.
roots_lines: Hebrew holelah (H1947) — madness, folly; the Preacher’s word throughout Ecclesiastes.
Hebrew shiggaon (H7697) — raving madness; the LORD shall smite thee with madness (Deuteronomy 28:28).
Greek paraphronia (G3913) — being beside one’s mind; the madness of the prophet (2 Peter 2:16).
Greek mania (G3130) — madness; Festus to Paul, much learning doth make thee mad (Acts 26:24).
Greek anoia (G454) — want of understanding, folly; they were filled with madness (Luke 6:11).
usage: Madness is in their heart while they live (Ecclesiastes 9:3) — a verdict on the race, not on the deranged few.
The LORD shall smite thee with madness (Deuteronomy 28:28) — the mind itself among the covenant curses.
The dumb ass… forbad the madness of the prophet (2 Peter 2:16) — a man who would not hear God heard a donkey.

etymology: From Saxon saed, sated, full, heavy — the older sense being weighty or grave rather than merely sorrowful. Webster 1828: sorrowful; heavy; serious; grave; and, in an older use, firm or solid. Scripture uses it chiefly of the countenance, where grief becomes visible.
biblical_def: Sad in the Authorized Version almost always attaches to a face, because Scripture treats grief as something that shows. Joseph, himself a prisoner, notices it in two fellow prisoners and asks about it: And Joseph came in unto them in the morning, and looked upon them, and, behold, they were sad (Genesis 40:6) — a man in a dungeon paying attention to other men’s faces, which is how the whole chain of his deliverance begins. Hannah’s sadness lifts before her circumstances change: after Eli blesses her, the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad (1 Samuel 1:18). She has not yet conceived; she has been heard. Nehemiah’s sadness in the presence of a Persian king was dangerous, and he says so: Why is thy countenance sad, seeing thou art not sick? this is nothing else but sorrow of heart. Then I was very sore afraid (Nehemiah 2:2). And the word records two failures to receive Christ: the rich young man, he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions (Mark 10:22), and the two on the Emmaus road, whom the risen Lord found sad because they had not yet understood that the Christ must suffer (Luke 24:17).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SAD as sorrowful; affected with grief; heavy in spirit; also serious, grave, or not light; and in an older and now rare sense, firm, solid, or heavy in substance.
webster_full: SAD, a. — Sorrowful; affected with grief; cast down in spirits.
Serious; grave; not light or volatile; as, a sad and weighty matter.
Causing sorrow; calamitous; as, a sad accident, or a sad reverse.
In an old and rare sense, heavy, firm, or close in texture; as, sad bread — the root meaning of full or sated.
From Saxon saed, sated, heavy — connected with satiate and with the Latin satis, enough.
scriptures: Genesis 40:6
And Joseph came in unto them in the morning, and looked upon them, and, behold, they were sad.
1 Samuel 1:18
And she said, Let thine handmaid find grace in thy sight. So the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad.
Nehemiah 2:2
Wherefore the king said unto me, Why is thy countenance sad, seeing thou art not sick? this is nothing else but sorrow of heart. Then I was very sore afraid,
Mark 10:22
And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions.
Luke 24:17
And he said unto them, What manner of communications are these that ye have one to another, as ye walk, and are sad?
corruption_summary: Mark 10:22 records the only person in the Gospels who came to Christ eagerly and went away sad, and the modern habit of presenting the gospel as an addition to a life rather than a claim upon it has removed the possibility of that outcome.
corruption_paragraphs: The young man ran to Christ, knelt, and asked the right question, and Mark says the Lord beholding him loved him before naming the one thing he lacked. The demand was total and particular: sell what thou hast, give to the poor, come and follow. He went away sad, and the Lord let him go without softening the terms or calling after him with a smaller offer. Modern evangelism is largely constructed to prevent this scene. The claim is presented as an addition to the hearer’s existing life, the cost is postponed to a later stage of discipleship, and no one is ever permitted to leave sorrowful. But a gospel that cannot produce Mark 10:22 is not the gospel Christ preached, and the church that never sees anyone walk away is probably not asking anyone for anything.

The other three uses supply the balance, and it is a real one. Hannah’s countenance was no more sad before her circumstances changed at all — sorrow lifted by being heard, which is what prayer often accomplishes and what it always accomplishes eventually. Joseph, in prison, looked at two men’s faces and asked why they were sad, and God used the question. And the risen Christ walked seven miles with two sad disciples and began not with comfort but with a rebuke and an exposition: O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken… And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. Their sadness was cured by Scripture opened, and their hearts burned before they knew who He was.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra (H7451), evil, and of the countenance, sad or downcast; zaaph (H2196), to be sad, to rage; Greek stugnazo (G4768), to become gloomy, to lower as a sky; skuthropos (G4659), of a sad countenance.
roots_lines: Hebrew zaaph (H2196) — to be out of humour, sad, vexed; behold, they were sad (Genesis 40:6).
Hebrew panim ra — literally an evil face; the idiom for a downcast countenance in Nehemiah 2:2.
Greek stugnazo (G4768) — to become gloomy, as a darkening sky; he was sad at that saying (Mark 10:22).
Greek skuthropos (G4659) — of a gloomy countenance; the two on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:17), and the hypocrites of Matthew 6:16.
Greek lupeo (G3076) — to grieve, to make sorrowful; the New Testament’s general verb of sorrow.
usage: Behold, they were sad (Genesis 40:6) — a prisoner noticing other prisoners’ faces.
Her countenance was no more sad (1 Samuel 1:18) — sorrow lifted before circumstances changed.
He was sad at that saying, and went away grieved (Mark 10:22) — the one man who came running and left sorrowful.

etymology: From Middle English pange, probably related to prong and to the Saxon pyngan, to prick. Webster 1828: extreme pain; anguish; agony of body or mind; particularly, the throes of childbirth. Scripture uses it almost exclusively with the figure of travail.
biblical_def: Pangs in the prophets are travail pains, and the figure is chosen because such pain is sudden, unavoidable, escalating, and — crucially — productive. Isaiah announces the fall of Babylon in these terms: they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them; they shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth: they shall be amazed one at another; their faces shall be as flames (Isaiah 13:8). The men of a proud empire are described in the language of a labouring woman, and there is no dignity left in the picture. The prophet then reports the same pain in himself as he receives the vision: Therefore are my loins filled with pain: pangs have taken hold upon me, as the pangs of a woman that travaileth: I was bowed down at the hearing of it; I was dismayed at the seeing of it (Isaiah 21:3) — a true prophet is not detached from the judgment he announces. Jeremiah addresses a king secure in his cedar palace: O inhabitant of Lebanon, that makest thy nest in the cedars, how gracious shalt thou be when pangs come upon thee, the pain as of a woman in travail! (Jeremiah 22:23). Comfort and elevation are no protection when the pangs begin.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PANG as extreme pain; anguish; agony of body or mind; particularly, a sudden paroxysm of extreme pain, as the throes of childbirth or the pangs of death.
webster_full: PANG, n. — Extreme pain; anguish; agony of body; a sudden and severe paroxysm of suffering.
Agony of mind; as, the pangs of remorse, or the pangs of guilt.
Particularly, the throes of childbirth; the pains of travail.
The pangs of death — the final agony; used in Scripture of the pains from which Christ was loosed in the resurrection.
From Middle English pange, allied to prong and to the Saxon pyngan, to prick or sting.
scriptures: Isaiah 13:8
And they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them; they shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth: they shall be amazed one at another; their faces shall be as flames.
Isaiah 21:3
Therefore are my loins filled with pain: pangs have taken hold upon me, as the pangs of a woman that travaileth: I was bowed down at the hearing of it; I was dismayed at the seeing of it.
Jeremiah 22:23
O inhabitant of Lebanon, that makest thy nest in the cedars, how gracious shalt thou be when pangs come upon thee, the pain as of a woman in travail!
Isaiah 35:10
And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 21:3 shows a prophet in physical anguish over a judgment he must announce, which rebukes the relish with which some preachers deliver warnings of wrath and the silence with which most now decline to deliver them at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is a startling piece of self-disclosure. Isaiah has been given a vision of Babylon’s fall — the fall of the empire that oppressed his people — and his response is loins filled with pain, pangs like a woman in travail, bowed down and dismayed. He does not enjoy it. Jeremiah says the same of himself: Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people (Jeremiah 9:1). Paul had great heaviness and continual sorrow in his heart for Israel. Set against this, a ministry that announces judgment with satisfaction has not understood the office, and a ministry that will not announce it at all has abandoned the office. The prophets did both things at once: they told the truth, and it cost them.

The travail figure carries its own hope and Scripture develops it deliberately. Pain like this is not aimless; it produces. The Lord used the same image of His disciples’ grief: A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come: but as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world (John 16:21). Romans 8:22 says the whole creation travails together until now, waiting for the manifestation of the sons of God. And Acts 2:24 says God raised Christ, having loosed the pains of death — the same word — because it was not possible that He should be holden of it. Isaiah 35:10 names the end: sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
roots_summary: Hebrew chebel (H2256), a pang, a birth-pain; tsir (H6735), a pang, a writhing; chil (H2342), to twist, to writhe, to travail; Greek odin (G5604), a birth-pang.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsir (H6735) — a pang, a writhing; pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them (Isaiah 13:8).
Hebrew chebel (H2256) — a birth-pang, a cord; when pangs come upon thee (Jeremiah 22:23).
Hebrew chil (H2342) — to writhe, to travail; as a woman that travaileth throughout the prophets.
Greek odin (G5604) — a birth-pang; the pains of death loosed at the resurrection (Acts 2:24), and the beginning of sorrows (Matthew 24:8).
Greek sunodino (G4944) — to travail together; the creation groaning in Romans 8:22.
usage: Pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them (Isaiah 13:8) — a proud empire described as a woman in labour.
Pangs have taken hold upon me (Isaiah 21:3) — the prophet in anguish over the judgment he must announce.
How gracious shalt thou be when pangs come upon thee (Jeremiah 22:23) — a cedar nest is no protection.

etymology: From dread, Saxon draedan, to fear greatly, and the suffix -ful. Webster 1828: impressing dread; terrible; awful; venerable in the highest degree. The older English sense includes reverence, which is why Scripture can call God dreadful as praise.
biblical_def: Dreadful in the Authorized Version is not simply frightening; it carries the older sense of that which rightly commands awe, and Scripture uses it of God, of a place, of a day, and of a beast. Jacob wakes at Bethel and says the thing that the modern religious vocabulary has almost lost the power to say: And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven (Genesis 28:17). He is not complaining; he is worshipping. Daniel opens his great prayer of confession by naming God in the same register, and joining the terror to the covenant in one breath: O Lord, the great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy to them that love him, and to them that keep his commandments (Daniel 9:4). Malachi closes the Old Testament pointing forward: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). And Daniel uses the word for the fourth beast of the night vision: a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth (Daniel 7:7).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DREADFUL as impressing dread; terrible; frightful; formidable; and, in the older and higher sense, awful, venerable in the highest degree — that which is to be regarded with reverential fear.
webster_full: DREADFUL, a. — Impressing dread; terrible; frightful; formidable to the mind.
Awful; venerable in the highest degree; to be regarded with reverential fear.
Inspiring awe by greatness, majesty, or holiness, as well as by danger.
Applied in Scripture to God, to His day, to holy places, and to the visions of judgment.
From dread, Saxon draedan, to fear greatly, and -ful, full of.
scriptures: Genesis 28:17
And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
Daniel 9:4
And I prayed unto the LORD my God, and made my confession, and said, O Lord, the great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy to them that love him, and to them that keep his commandments;
Malachi 4:5
Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD:
Daniel 7:7

After this I saw in the night visions, and behold a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth: it devoured and brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with the feet of it: and it was diverse from all the beasts that were before it; and it had ten horns.
corruption_summary: Daniel 9:4 addresses God as great and dreadful in the same clause that names His covenant mercy, and the modern devotional register — which knows how to say tender and has no idea how to say dreadful — has quietly lost half of the biblical doctrine of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The two halves of Daniel’s address belong together and neither is safe alone. He prays to the great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy to them that love him, and the prayer that follows is one of the most thorough confessions in Scripture. A God who is only dreadful cannot be approached; a God who is only tender need not be confessed to. The contemporary evangelical vocabulary has almost entirely lost the first term. God is described as loving, welcoming, and near, and rarely as the One before whom Isaiah cried Woe is me! for I am undone, before whom John fell at His feet as dead, and of whom Hebrews 12:29 says our God is a consuming fire. The result is not warmer worship but thinner worship, since the tenderness means little if it is a temperament rather than a condescension.

Genesis 28:17 shows what recovery looks like. Jacob, a deceiver running from a brother he had cheated, wakes from a dream of angels and says How dreadful is this place! — and calls it the house of God and the gate of heaven in the same sentence. Awe and welcome are not alternatives to be balanced but a single response to a single God. Malachi 4:5 sets the same word over the last day, and it is the last verse but one in the Old Testament: the coming of the LORD is great and dreadful, and the promise attached is that hearts will be turned lest the earth be smitten with a curse.
roots_summary: Hebrew yare (H3372), to fear, to reverence; nora (H3372 niphal participle), dreadful, to be feared; emah (H367), terror; Greek phoberos (G5398), fearful, terrible.
roots_lines: Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear, to revere; its participle nora is the dreadful of Genesis 28:17 and Daniel 9:4.
Hebrew emah (H367) — terror, dread; a horror of great darkness fell upon him (Genesis 15:12).
Hebrew dechal (H1763) — Aramaic, to be afraid; dreadful and terrible of the fourth beast (Daniel 7:7).
Greek phoberos (G5398) — fearful, terrible; a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Hebrews 10:31).
Greek phobos (G5401) — fear; the root of the fear of the Lord in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 7:1).
usage: How dreadful is this place! (Genesis 28:17) — not a complaint but an act of worship.
The great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy (Daniel 9:4) — terror and covenant mercy in one clause.
The great and dreadful day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5) — the last word of the Old Testament but one.
